## Proof

**Setup.** Let $\lambda_n = np_n$ with $\lambda_n \to \lambda > 0$, and set
$$a_n := (1-s)\frac{\lambda_n}{n} = (1-s)p_n, \qquad b_n := (1-s)\frac{\lambda}{n}.$$
We must bound $\left|(1-a_n)^n - (1-b_n)^n\right|$.

**Key identity (telescoping / geometric factorization).** For any $x,y \in \mathbb{C}$,
$$x^n - y^n = (x-y)\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}x^{n-1-k}y^k,$$
hence
$$|x^n - y^n| \le |x-y|\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}|x|^{n-1-k}|y|^k. \tag{1}$$

**Bounding the factors.** Take $x = 1-a_n = 1-(1-s)p_n$ and $y = 1-b_n = 1-(1-s)\tfrac{\lambda}{n}$. For the generating-function setting we have $s \in [0,1]$, $p_n \in [0,1]$, $\lambda > 0$, so
$$0 \le a_n = (1-s)p_n \le 1, \qquad 0 \le b_n = (1-s)\tfrac{\lambda}{n} \le 1 \quad(\text{for } n \text{ large}).$$
Consequently $x,y \in [0,1]$, giving $|x|\le 1$ and $|y|\le 1$. Therefore
$$\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}|x|^{n-1-k}|y|^k \le \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}1 = n. \tag{2}$$

**Applying (1) with (2).** Since $|x-y| = |a_n - b_n| = |1-s|\,\dfrac{|\lambda_n - \lambda|}{n}$,
$$\left|(1-a_n)^n - (1-b_n)^n\right| \le |1-s|\,\frac{|\lambda_n-\lambda|}{n}\cdot n = |1-s|\,|\lambda_n - \lambda|. \tag{3}$$

**Taking the limit.** Passing to the limit in (3) and using the hypothesis $\lambda_n \to \lambda$,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\left(1-(1-s)\frac{\lambda_n}{n}\right)^n - \left(1-(1-s)\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^n\right| \le \lim_{n\to\infty}|1-s|\,|\lambda_n-\lambda| = |1-s|\cdot 0 = 0. \tag{4}$$

**Interpretation (Poisson limit).** The left-hand term $(1-(1-s)\tfrac{\lambda_n}{n})^n = (1-(1-s)p_n)^n$ is exactly the probability generating function of $X_n \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p_n)$, evaluated at $s$. The right-hand term satisfies
$$\left(1-(1-s)\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^n \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{} e^{-(1-s)\lambda} = e^{\lambda(s-1)},$$
which is the probability generating function of $Y \sim \mathrm{Pois}(\lambda)$. Inequality (4) shows the binomial generating functions converge to the Poisson generating function, and since a distribution on $\mathbb{N}_0$ is uniquely determined by its pgf on $[0,1]$, this yields $X_n \xrightarrow{d} Y$ — the law of small numbers. $\blacksquare$
